label: Galatians 1:1
text: Paul opens with apostolos — from apo ("from") and stello ("send") — the word for an envoy sent out with credentials, not a volunteer carrying a message. Everything else in the verse is Paul defending those credentials. He is exact with his prepositions: apo marks an ultimate source ("not from men"), while dia marks an intermediate channel or agent ("neither by man"). So he denies two separate things — that mankind is the fountainhead of his commission, and that any human hand was the pipeline through which it reached him. The word shifts from the plural "men" (anthropos, the human race in general) to the singular "man" because in Paul's world a body's authority was typically exercised through one representative — the Senate through the emperor, the Sanhedrin through the high priest — so ruling out even a single human intermediary is a sweeping claim. Then dia returns, now positively: "through Jesus Christ and God the Father," both names governed by one preposition, meaning they are not agent-then-source in sequence but a single, joint origin. Tacking on "who raised him from the dead" quietly sets Paul's commission apart from the Twelve's: theirs came from Jesus in his humbled, pre-resurrection state; his came from the risen, glorified Christ.
translation: Paul, a commissioned envoy — not from men as a source, and not even through a man as a channel, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him up out from among the dead.

label: Galatians 1:2
text: Naming "all the brothers with me" alongside himself is not sentimental filler. In ancient letters, names added to the opening address functioned as co-signers lending authority to what followed, unlike names tacked onto a closing greeting, which were simply expressions of affection. Paul wants the Galatians to know this isn't one man's private opinion. Then comes the address itself, strikingly bare — no commendation, not even the word "saints," unlike every other Pauline opening, even to the badly-behaved Corinthians. The silence is itself a rebuke. "Church" translates ekklesia, built on a verb meaning "to call out": in secular Greek it named a citizen assembly summoned for public business, and Paul repurposes it for a called-out gathering of believers.
translation: And all the brothers with me, to the assemblies of Galatia.

label: Galatians 1:3
text: The formula "grace to you and peace" is Paul's standard opening, but it lands with special weight here, aimed at Galatians being talked out of grace by legalists. Both "God the Father" and "the Lord Jesus Christ" sit under one governing preposition, apo, marking them as a single joint source — grace and peace do not come partly from one and partly from the other, but from both acting as one. The grace in view is the Spirit's ongoing enabling work in a believer's life, not merely the initial gift of salvation, and the peace is the settled inward peace that flows from that same ministry — exactly what the Galatians were trading away for self-effort under law.
translation: Grace to you, and peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

label: Galatians 1:4
text: "Gave himself for our sins" uses hyper, the preposition of substitution — the ordinary word for one person acting in another's place. It's the same word a professional scribe used when signing a document for an illiterate client: "I wrote in his place." Paul reaches for the strongest available term to say Christ stood in for us. "Deliver" is exaireo, to pluck out, to rescue by force — not a gentle removal but an extraction. And the "evil" of "this present evil world" is poneros, not kakos: kakos describes something rotten in itself, content to decay quietly, while poneros describes an active, contagious evil that isn't satisfied until it drags others down too. The present age isn't merely bad — it's aggressively, corrosively bad, and the legalism of the Judaizers belongs to that same corrupting system.
translation: Who gave himself in place of our sins, so that he might pluck us out from this present, actively corrupting age, according to the will of our God and Father.

label: Galatians 1:5
text: The doxology is brief, but "for ever and ever" repays a glance — literally "unto the ages of the ages," stacking the Greek word for a bounded era of time (aion) on top of itself to push duration past any measurable limit. It is the language of eternity built out of the language of epochs.
translation: To whom be the glory unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

label: Galatians 1:6–7
text: "I marvel" is thaumazo — real astonishment, the reaction of someone who expected better. "Removed" translates metatithemi, elsewhere used for a turncoat switching sides, but Paul deliberately keeps it in the present tense rather than the perfect — a calculated hope, since the defection is still in motion, not yet a settled, finished fact. "So soon" (tacheos) underlines the speed of it. Then comes a play on two Greek words for "another." Heteros means another of a different, often inferior kind (our word "heterodox" comes from it); allos means simply one more of the same kind. Paul says the Galatians are turning to a heteros gospel — different in kind, and evil in kind — which sets up the paradox that follows: it isn't even an allos gospel, "not another" at all, because a message of salvation by works cannot logically be called good news and still count as gospel. "Trouble" (tarasso, present tense) describes ongoing mental agitation — these agitators are still actively at work as Paul writes — and "pervert" (metastrepho) doesn't mean bend or distort; it means reverse into the opposite.
translation: I am marveling that so quickly you are shifting away from him who called you in the sphere of Christ's grace, to a different-in-kind gospel — not that there is another gospel of the same kind, only there are some who are continually troubling you and wanting to reverse the gospel of Christ into its opposite.

label: Galatians 1:8
text: "But" is alla, the sharper of Greek's two adversatives — Paul is not softening anything. He includes "we" (himself and his co-workers) to show this is not one teacher's pet doctrine against another's, but truth against error itself. "Preach a gospel" translates the single verb euangelizomai, "to announce good news"; Paul had a plain word for "proclaim" available (kerysso) and passed it over for the word that specifically means to evangelize. "Than" renders par' ho, literally "beside which" — not simply "against" but "overstepping the boundary of," moving into new, foreign territory. "Accursed" is anathema, a word used in the Greek Old Testament for something devoted to destruction because it is hateful to God — not church discipline (angels cannot be excommunicated) but the language of ultimate spiritual ruin.
translation: But even if we, or an angel out of heaven, should announce good news to you beyond the boundary of what we announced to you, let him be accursed.

label: Galatians 1:9
text: "As we said before" uses a verb meaning "to say beforehand," pointing to an earlier warning already given, not a restatement of the sentence just written. And where the surrounding verses lean on the perfect tense — completed actions with abiding results — verse 9 shifts its conditional: not the hypothetical ean but ei, the "if" of a condition assumed to be actually true. Paul isn't entertaining a possibility; he's stating a fact. "Received" is paralambano, elsewhere used of a host warmly welcoming a guest — the Galatians had once taken the true gospel to their hearts eagerly, which makes their present drift worse.
translation: As we have said before, now again I am saying: if, as is the case, anyone announces good news to you beyond what you took to yourselves so eagerly, let him be accursed.

label: Galatians 1:10
text: "Persuade" is peitho, more precisely "to win over, to conciliate" -- Paul is answering a whispered charge that he shapes his message to flatter people. "Or" translates a word meaning "rather than," which shows exactly what the slander claimed: that he cared more about pleasing men than pleasing God. Paul then pivots toward the origin of his gospel with "certify" (gnorizo), which doesn't mean he's telling the Galatians something new -- it means driving home, emphatically, something they already knew. He calls them "brothers," from adelphos, literally "of the same womb," kin through a shared new birth. "Is not after man" uses kata, a preposition whose root idea is "down," carrying the sense of "measured by" or "controlled by" -- Paul's gospel isn't just non-human in origin, it isn't human in standard or character either.
translation: For am I now trying to win over men, or God? Or am I seeking to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a slave of Christ. For I make known to you, brothers, that the gospel announced by me is not, as to its very nature, a human thing.

label: Galatians 1:12
text: Greek verbs already carry their subject built in, so when a writer adds the separate pronoun "I" (ego), it signals deliberate emphasis. Paul underlines his own case against the Twelve's: he "received" (paralambano, taking something passed along directly from another person) nothing, and was "taught" (didasko, learning by instruction) nothing. Instead he got a "revelation," apokalypsis, the uncovering of something previously hidden, an unveiling accompanied by real understanding, not just a flash of insight. And the phrase "of Jesus Christ" is a subjective genitive: Christ is the one doing the revealing, not merely the content revealed.
translation: For neither did I myself receive it from a man, nor was I taught it, but I got it through an uncovering by Jesus Christ.

label: Galatians 1:13
text: "Conversation" is old English for "way of life," translating anastrophe. "The Jews' religion" renders one word, Ioudaismos — likely coined with a note of outsider contempt, much the way "Christianoi" was first used of believers before both groups adopted their labels as badges of honor. The verbs "persecuted" and "wasted" are imperfect tense — not a single episode but sustained, continuous action stretching right up to his conversion. "Wasted" (portheo) is a violent word, elsewhere used of the sacking of cities, not mere harassment.
translation: For you heard of my former way of life in Judaism, that I was, beyond measure, continually persecuting the church of God and continually devastating it.

label: Galatians 1:14
text: "Profited" translates prokopto, literally "to cut a path forward" — the image of a pioneer hacking through undergrowth ahead of everyone else, not simply doing well in class. Paul means he was out ahead of his peers, blazing trail in Jewish scholarship and zeal. "Tradition" is paradosis, "something handed down," and Paul is careful to root his old zeal in ancestral tradition rather than in the Mosaic law itself, since the Pharisaic traditions had grown up alongside the law and, in places, buried it.
translation: And I was continually cutting ahead, beyond many of my own age among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions handed down from my fathers.

label: Galatians 1:15–16
text: "Separated" is aphorizo, "to mark off within a boundary" — not physical removal from the womb, but being set apart for a purpose before birth, the same idea used elsewhere of Samson and John the Baptist. "Reveal his Son in me" uses apokalypto again — an inward, subjective unveiling within Paul, not an outward disclosure of Christ to the world through Paul, which would require the preposition "through" rather than "in." This distinguishes the revelation from the earlier, external, ocular vision on the Damascus road; this was an inward apprehension, likely during the silent stretch that followed. "Conferred" is prosanatithemi, a word used elsewhere of consulting oracles or soothsayers — Paul says, pointedly, that he did not go looking for anyone else's opinion on what had just happened to him.
translation: But when it was the good pleasure of him who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me through his grace, to unveil his Son within me, so that I might announce him as good news among the Gentiles, immediately I did not confer with flesh and blood.

label: Galatians 1:17
text: "Went up" is anerchomai, the standard word for approaching Jerusalem, a city on high ground both geographically and religiously, so that journeys toward it were always described as "going up" and departures as "going down." "Before me" places the temporal marker pro ("before," in time) next to "apostles," quietly granting that the Twelve held the same office Paul claims, just earlier. "Arabia" transliterates a word meaning roughly "an arid, sparsely peopled place" — Paul went looking for solitude, not an audience.
translation: Neither did I go up to Jerusalem, to those who were apostles before me; but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.

label: Galatians 1:18
text: "See" translates historeo, "to inquire into, to visit for the purpose of getting acquainted" — a deliberate, purposeful visit, not a chance encounter. "Peter" transliterates the Greek petros, "rock," itself a rendering of the Aramaic Kephas that Paul actually writes — a rock by either name. Fifteen days is mentioned to make the brevity itself the point: nowhere near long enough to have learned the gospel from him.
translation: Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to get acquainted with Kephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days.

label: Galatians 1:19
text: The Greek construction counts James among the apostles Paul saw, though he was not one of the Twelve — a natural-born brother of Jesus, son of Joseph and Mary, recognized as an apostle without having been among the original appointees, likely after witnessing the risen Christ himself.
translation: But I saw none of the other apostles, except James, the brother of the Lord.

label: Galatians 1:20
text: The oath — "before God, I do not lie" — answers a specific slander: the Judaizers had apparently spread word that Paul spent extensive time under the Twelve's tutelage in Jerusalem. The strength of the sworn denial is proportional to how damaging that lie was to his whole argument.
translation: Now the things I am writing to you — behold, before God, I am not lying.

label: Galatians 1:21
text: "Regions" is klimata, literally the sloping tracts of land running down from the mountains toward the sea, a geographical term for northern Syria and eastern Cilicia. Syria is named first because Paul's work in Antioch preceded his time in Tarsus, and because Cilicia was administratively subordinate to Syria under Rome.
translation: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.

label: Galatians 1:22
text: "Was unknown" describes a continuous state — literally "I remained unknown" — not a momentary gap that quickly closed. "By face" specifies exactly what kind of ignorance is meant: they simply didn't recognize him on sight. And "in Christ," attached to "the churches of Judea," distinguishes these believing assemblies from the ordinary Jewish synagogues of the same region.
translation: And I remained, in person, unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.

label: Galatians 1:23
text: "Were hearing" is imperfect — they kept on hearing this report repeatedly, not just once. "Destroyed" is portheo again, the same violent word from verse 13, describing not the historical fact of Paul having once wrecked the church but the ongoing process he used to pursue as a persecutor, now flipped completely into ongoing gospel proclamation.
translation: Only, they kept on hearing: 'He who used to persecute us is now announcing as good news the faith he once was devastating.'

label: Galatians 1:24
text: "Glorified" is imperfect too — a continuing, repeated response, not a single moment of praise. "In me" uses en in the sense of ground or basis: Paul's changed life was the occasion, the reason, for their glorifying God, not merely the setting in which it happened.
translation: And they kept on glorifying God on account of me.

label: Galatians 2:1
text: "Took" is synparalambano, "to take along as a companion" — and bringing Titus, an uncircumcised Gentile, up to Jerusalem was a deliberate provocation, turning him into a living test case for the whole controversy about to be argued.
translation: Then, after the space of fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along also.

label: Galatians 2:2
text: "By revelation" is kata, "in accordance with" — not necessarily the sole cause of the trip, since Acts records the Antioch church commissioning him too, but Paul adds that the Spirit independently confirmed the same direction. "Communicate" is anatithemi, "to lay something out for others' consideration" — Paul presented his gospel for a hearing, not for correction. "Of reputation" translates a participle of dokeo, "to be reputed, held in esteem," a genuine term of honor for James, Peter, and John, with no sarcasm implied by the Greek itself. "Run in vain" draws on the footrace, in the present subjunctive, expressing a live, ongoing fear that his mission work could still be undercut — not that it already had failed.
translation: And I went up in accordance with a revelation, and I laid before them the gospel that I am preaching among the Gentiles — privately, before those of recognized standing — for fear that I might be running, or have run, for nothing.

label: Galatians 2:3
text: "Being" carries concessive force — "although being" a Gentile. "Compelled" denies not the attempt but its success: real pressure was applied to force circumcision on Titus, and it failed.
translation: But not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, Greek though he was.

label: Galatians 2:4
text: "Brought in unawares" is pareisago, "to bring in alongside" — used elsewhere of smuggling hostile agents into a city through a friendly faction inside the walls. "Who" translates hoitines, a pronoun flagging not mere identity but character: these people were running true to type. "Came in privily" (pareiserchomai) is aorist with the force of a pluperfect, describing an earlier, gradual infiltration. "Spy out" (kataskopeo) is a straightforward military-espionage word. "Bring into bondage" (katadouloo) means to reduce to utter slavery, put in the future tense to mark not a vague wish but a plan its authors expected to succeed.
translation: It was because of false brothers who had been secretly brought in — the kind who had stolen in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, meaning to reduce us to abject slavery.

label: Galatians 2:5
text: "Gave place" is eiko, "to yield." "Subjection" (hypotage) describes an act of voluntary submission, which Paul refuses to make even briefly — the point being that nothing was ever imposed on him, because he never yielded anything to begin with.
translation: To them we did not yield in submission, not for a single hour, so that the truth of the gospel might continue to abide with you.

label: Galatians 2:6
text: "Of reputation" is the same dokeo-word from verse 2, no irony intended. "Added" is prosanatithemi, the same verb Paul used in 1:16 for "conferred," now negated: the Jerusalem leaders imparted nothing to him, exactly as he had imparted nothing to them beforehand. "Maketh no matter" is diaphero, "to matter, to make a difference" — Paul flatly says their former status changes nothing about his commission, since it came from God directly.
translation: But from those who were of reputation — whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not receive a man's face — those of reputation added nothing to me.

label: Galatians 2:7
text: "Committed" is pepisteumai, perfect tense, a technical administrative term used in the imperial bureaucracy for someone formally and permanently entrusted with a responsibility. Paul is not describing two different gospels for two different audiences — "the gospel to the uncircumcision" and "the gospel to the circumcision" are the same message, entrusted to different messengers for different fields.
translation: But on the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with it to the circumcised.

label: Galatians 2:8
text: "Wrought" is energeo, describing God's actual operative power at work — and notably it is not paired here with the preposition "in," as it usually is when Scripture describes the Spirit's inward work in a believer. This is God's outward blessing on their preaching, not an inward transformation being described. "Peter" and "me" sit in the dative, the case marking whose interest an action serves: God worked for Peter, and God worked for Paul, in the same way.
translation: For he who worked effectively for Peter with a view to an apostleship to the circumcised, worked effectively for me also, with a view to the Gentiles.

label: Galatians 2:9
text: "Pillars" (stylos) is architectural language borrowed for people — the church pictured as a temple, and these three men as its structural supports. The right hand given in pledge was a widespread ancient gesture of ratified partnership, found on treaties and coins alike. "Fellowship" is koinonia, a shared enterprise, a partnership — here specifically a partnership in preaching the same gospel to different fields.
translation: And when James, Kephas, and John — who were of reputation as pillars — recognized the grace given to me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of partnership, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.

label: Galatians 2:10
text: "Remember" (mnemoneuo) is used here in an unusual sense — not simply "recall" but "care for, provide for." "Forward" is spoudazo, meaning eager, diligent effort, not just willingness — Paul describes sustained activity, not a passing intention.
translation: Only, that we should keep on remembering the poor — the very thing I was, in fact, eager and diligent to do.

label: Galatians 2:11
text: "Withstood" is anthistemi, "to set oneself against," a verb that usually implies the other side struck first — in Paul's telling, Peter was the aggressor, even if unintentionally. "He was to be blamed" renders a perfect participle with an imperfect verb, literally "he stood condemned," describing an ongoing state of standing under judgment in the eyes of the Antioch believers, not a single accusation.
translation: But when Kephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.

label: Galatians 2:12
text: "Did eat" is imperfect — a settled habit, not a one-time meal. "Withdrew" (hypostello) is a military term for pulling troops back under cover, or a sailor's term for furling a sail — imperfect as well, describing a gradual retreat rather than a sudden break. "Separated" (aphorizo) marks the final, completed severing that followed the gradual withdrawal.
translation: For before certain men came from James, he was in the habit of eating with the Gentiles; but when they came, he began drawing back and separating himself, fearing those of the circumcision.

label: Galatians 2:13
text: "Dissembled" is hypokrinomai, literally "to answer from under [a mask]" — the root of our word "hypocrite," the language of an actor playing a part that conceals his true face. "Carried away" pictures Barnabas swept along with the rest, Paul's own closest partner in Gentile ministry caught in the same pretense.
translation: And the rest of the Jews also played along with his pretense, so that even Barnabas was swept along with their pretense.

label: Galatians 2:14
text: "Walked uprightly" translates orthopodeo, literally "walk with straight feet" — the image of an honest, undeviating course. "According to" (pros) narrows the charge precisely: not that Peter's whole life was crooked, but that his stance toward gospel truth, specifically, was not straight. "Livest" is present tense, describing a settled pattern rather than his behavior at that literal moment.
translation: But when I saw that they were not walking a straight course with reference to the truth of the gospel, I said to Kephas in front of everyone: 'If you, a Jew, are habitually living like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?'

label: Galatians 2:15
text: The pronoun "we" is emphatic — Greek verbs already carry their subject, so adding it deliberately draws a sharp line between "us" (Jews by birth) and Gentile "sinners," a phrase Paul is using ironically, borrowing the very language of Pharisaic contempt he once wielded himself.
translation: We ourselves are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles.

label: Galatians 2:16
text: "Law" here means divine law treated purely as a legal system of merit — obey and be approved, disobey and be condemned. Paul's own life had proven the system fails even its most devoted keepers. "Justified" is dikaioo, sharing a root with dikaiosyne, "righteousness" — the act of declaring, not gradually making, someone righteous. "By" before "faith" translates dia, marking the channel through which that verdict comes.
translation: Knowing that a man is not declared righteous by works of law, but only through faith in Jesus Christ, we too put our trust in Christ Jesus, so that we might be declared righteous by faith in Christ, and not by works of law — because by works of law no flesh will be declared righteous.

label: Galatians 2:17
text: "If" is ei, marking a real, fulfilled condition, not a hypothetical. The logic runs: seeking justification in Christ puts a Jew in the very category, "sinner," he'd normally reserve for Gentiles, since the seeking itself admits works never justified him. "By" here is en, better read as the sphere in which justification happens — Christ himself is the space within which a believer is declared righteous, not merely the tool by which it is accomplished.
translation: But if, in seeking to be declared righteous in Christ, we ourselves also were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Away with the thought!

label: Galatians 2:18
text: "Build" (oikodomeo) and "destroy" (kataluo) are architectural opposites applied to legal validity — to build is to declare something standing and binding, to destroy is to strip it of force. Paul pictures himself tearing the law down as a means of acceptance with God, then rebuilding it by going back to it, an act that would prove him the very transgressor he claims not to be. "Transgressor" is parabates, someone who crosses a known boundary, sharper than the ordinary word for sinner (hamartolos, "one who misses a mark") because it names a willful, informed violation.
translation: For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I demonstrate myself to be a transgressor.

label: Galatians 2:19
text: The emphatic ego ("I," myself) singles this out as Paul's own experience, not a general rule for everyone. "Died to the law through the law" is a paradox: the law's own penalty, satisfied in Christ's death, is what ends the law's claim on the believer — the law itself supplies the very means of escaping it.
translation: For I, through the law, died to the law, so that I might live to God.

label: Galatians 2:20
text: "Am crucified" is perfect tense, a completed past event with results still standing in the present — Paul's identification with Christ's death is a settled, finished fact whose benefits he keeps drawing on. "Yet not I" marks the swap of a self-directed life for a Christ-indwelt one, not the annihilation of the person but a change in what powers him.
translation: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith — the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself in my place.

label: Galatians 2:21
text: "Frustrate" is atheteo, "to set aside something established, to void it, to strip it of force" — the identical verb Paul later uses for annulling a legal covenant in 3:15. Adding works to grace does exactly that to grace, nullifying it, since grace by definition asks nothing in payment. "In vain" is dorean, literally "without a cause, gratuitously, for nothing" — if law-keeping could justify, Christ's death would have had no reason to happen.
translation: I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through law, then Christ died for nothing.

label: Galatians 3:1
text: "Foolish" is anoetos — not simple ignorance but a failure to use one's own powers of perception, a moral dullness rather than an intellectual defect. "Bewitched" (baskaino) draws on the old superstition of the evil eye, framing their defection as if a malignant spell had been cast over them. "Set forth" is prographo, the standard word for posting a public notice, the same verb used of a father publicly disowning responsibility for a son's debts — Paul preached Christ's crucifixion as a placarded public announcement, impossible to miss. "Crucified" is perfect tense: not a dead figure frozen on a cross, but the living, risen Christ who still and permanently bears the marks of that crucifixion.
translation: O senseless Galatians, who has cast an evil eye on you — you, before whose very eyes Jesus Christ was publicly placarded as the crucified one?

label: Galatians 3:2
text: "Hearing of faith" translates akoe pisteos — akoe can mean either the act of hearing or the message heard, and context favors the latter: "the message that proclaims faith," set against a message of law-obedience. Paul narrows the whole argument down to one decisive test question.
translation: This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of law, or by the message that proclaims faith?

label: Galatians 3:3
text: "Made perfect" is epiteleo, "to bring to completion" — full spiritual maturity, not sinless perfection. "Flesh" here means the whole natural human capacity operating apart from the Spirit, mind, will, effort, resume, not merely the physical body. Paul's question turns on a jarring mismatch: begun by the Spirit, are they now trying to finish by self-effort?
translation: Are you so senseless? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being brought to completion by the flesh?

label: Galatians 3:4
text: The construction leaves room for doubt in Paul's own mind — "if indeed" — as though he can hardly believe the sufferings they endured for the gospel might really turn out to have been pointless.
translation: Did you suffer so many things for nothing — if it really was for nothing?

label: Galatians 3:5
text: "Ministereth" is epichoregeo, a vivid word originally tied to underwriting the costs of a theatrical chorus — "to supply abundantly, lavishly, at one's own expense." Both participles, "supplying" and "working," are present tense: this was still happening even as the Galatians drifted, God's hand still visibly active among them in spite of their defection.
translation: Does he then who is continually, abundantly supplying the Spirit to you, and continually working works of power among you, do this by works of law, or by the message that proclaims faith?

label: Galatians 3:6
text: "Accounted" is logizomai, a bookkeeping term — to credit something to an account, to enter it on deposit. Abraham's faith was not a meritorious deed that earned righteousness as wages; it was simply credited, entered to his account, as righteousness.
translation: Just as Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him, resulting in righteousness.

label: Galatians 3:7
text: "Therefore" (ara) draws the logical conclusion straight out of verse 6. "Children" is huioi, properly "sons," a status word, not a genealogical one — Paul's point is deliberately non-biological: the family line that matters runs through shared faith, not shared blood.
translation: You perceive, then, that those who are of faith — these are sons of Abraham.

label: Galatians 3:8
text: Paul personifies "the scripture," crediting it with foresight, a Jewish idiom for saying that what Scripture records, God himself foresaw and intended. The verb "would justify" is present tense, marking a timeless principle rather than a single past event: this is simply how God has always operated.
translation: And the scripture, foreseeing that God would declare the Gentiles righteous by faith, announced the good news beforehand to Abraham: 'In you all the nations will be blessed.'

label: Galatians 3:9
text: "Faithful Abraham" singles out the one trait that mattered, that he believed, even though Abraham had every worldly reason to trust his own resources instead; he was no simple nomad but a cultured, wealthy man who nonetheless staked everything on taking God at his word.
translation: So then, those who are of faith are being blessed together with believing Abraham.

label: Galatians 3:10
text: "Under curse" places the phrase in a kind of legal territory — hupo marking the sphere or jurisdiction a person is bound within. "Continueth" pictures the law as a bounded domain: stay inside it perfectly, or you're already outside it and cursed, since no one keeps it perfectly.
translation: For as many as are of works of law are under a curse; for it stands written: 'Cursed is everyone who does not keep on remaining in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.'

label: Galatians 3:11
text: "By the law" is en nomo, literally "in law," the same locative-of-sphere idea from verse 10. "Just" functions here as a forensic, legal term, the person accepted and approved by God's verdict, not a description of moral character. "Shall live" describes the result of that verdict, a new standing before God, not an infusion of new energy.
translation: Now that no one is declared righteous before God within the sphere of law is evident, because 'the righteous shall live by faith.'

label: Galatians 3:12
text: Paul sets law and faith up as two mutually exclusive operating principles, not two stages of one process. The quotation from Leviticus describes a righteousness that would come from perfectly doing what the law demands, a righteousness no fallen person can actually produce.
translation: And the law is not of faith; but 'the one who does them shall live by them.'

label: Galatians 3:13
text: "Redeemed" is exagorazo, not the ordinary word for buying (agorazo, to purchase in the marketplace) but "to buy someone out of the marketplace" entirely, so they can never be put up for sale again — a stronger, more final image than a simple purchase. "For us" is hyper again, the substitution word from 1:4: Christ took the curse's place, standing exactly where we stood.
translation: Christ bought us out from under the curse of the law, having become a curse in our place — for it stands written: 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.'

label: Galatians 3:14
text: Two purpose clauses, each beginning with hina ("in order that"), run in parallel: Christ's becoming a curse accomplishes both the extension of Abraham's blessing to the Gentiles and the giving of the Spirit to Jew and Gentile alike, received the same way, through faith.
translation: So that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

label: Galatians 3:15
text: "Covenant" translates diatheke, from a verb meaning "to place between," an arrangement one party binds himself to, not a will or testament here. "Confirmed" is kuroo, "to ratify," in the perfect tense, meaning the ratification is a closed, settled matter. Paul's point rests on ordinary legal custom: once such an agreement is sealed, no one unilaterally cancels it (atheteo, the same verb from 2:21) or adds new terms to it (diatasso).
translation: Brothers, I am speaking in a human way: even a man's covenant, once it has been ratified, no one sets aside or adds conditions to.

label: Galatians 3:16
text: "Seed" in the singular, in Hebrew idiom, ordinarily just means "descendants" collectively, but Paul presses the grammatical singular to make a theological point, reading it as pointing to one person specifically, Christ, rather than to many.
translation: Now to Abraham the promises were spoken, and to his seed. He does not say, 'and to seeds,' as referring to many, but as referring to one: 'and to your seed,' who is Christ.

label: Galatians 3:17
text: The 430 years, drawn from Exodus, does real argumentative work: a covenant ratified centuries earlier and left standing that whole time cannot be quietly cancelled by a law that shows up later. The longer the gap, the stronger the point.
translation: This is what I mean: a covenant already ratified by God, the law which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul, so as to make the promise void.

label: Galatians 3:18
text: "Gave" is charizomai, sharing a root with charis, "grace," a gift given purely out of the giver's own generosity, with no reciprocal terms attached, unlike a pledge made under a mutual bargain, for which Greek had an entirely different word. The perfect tense marks this as a past grant whose effect is still standing.
translation: For if the inheritance is from law, it is no longer from promise; but God has granted it to Abraham, as a gift of grace, through promise.

label: Galatians 3:19
text: "Because of transgressions" leans toward purpose rather than mere cause: the law was added to expose and define transgression. "Transgression" (parabasis) means stepping over a known boundary, sharper than the broader word for sin (hamartia, literally "missing a mark"), because a boundary has to be marked before it can be crossed — the law turns vague moral failure into a named, specific violation. "Added" (prostithemi) marks the law as a later, subordinate supplement, not a rival to the original promise, and its arrival through two intermediaries, angels and a mediator, quietly underscores its lesser standing next to the promise God gave Abraham directly, face to face.
translation: What then is the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made — arranged through angels, by the hand of a mediator.

label: Galatians 3:20
text: "Mediator" is mesites, someone who stands in the middle of two or more parties — the very structure of the word implies a go-between, and a go-between only exists where there is a bilateral arrangement. The law needed a mediator because it functions like a two-party contract, obligations on both sides. The promise needed none, because God simply acted, alone, unconditionally.
translation: Now a mediator is not of one party alone; but God is one.

label: Galatians 3:21
text: Paul poses the question as a false dilemma and rejects it. If a law existed capable of producing life, righteousness really would come from law-keeping, but no such law exists, since none of us can perfectly keep it. Law and promise aren't opposed; they simply operate in different domains, one exposing guilt, the other offering rescue.
translation: Is the law then against the promises of God? Away with the thought! For if a law had been given that was able to give life, righteousness would indeed have been by law.

label: Galatians 3:22
text: "Concluded" is synkleio, "to shut up together, to confine" — Paul pictures Scripture as a jailer, locking all of humanity without exception into the single cell of universal sin, leaving faith in Christ as the only door out.
translation: But the scripture has locked up all things together under sin, so that the promise, by faith in Jesus Christ, might be given to those who believe.

label: Galatians 3:23
text: "Kept" is phroureo, a garrison term, to guard under close watch, as a fortress holds prisoners. "Unto" is eis, better read "with a view to" than as a strict marker of time: the guarding had a purpose, driving people toward faith, not just marking time until it arrived. The definite article before "faith" ties this specifically to faith in the historic, already-accomplished Christ, distinct from Abraham's faith, which looked forward to a Christ not yet come.
translation: But before the faith came, we were kept in custody under law, locked up with a view to the faith that was about to be revealed.

label: Galatians 3:24
text: "Schoolmaster" badly translates paidagogos, which did not mean a teacher (that word was didaskalos) but a household slave assigned to escort and morally supervise a boy from about age six to sixteen, walking him to school, watching his behavior, never instructing him directly. The image grows straight out of "kept" (phroureo, "guard") in the verse before: the law functioned as a strict, low-ranking guardian for a minor, not a teacher imparting content.
translation: So that the law became our guardian until Christ, so that we might be declared righteous by faith.

label: Galatians 3:25
text: The definite article before "faith" again ties this to the specific, historic faith already discussed — its arrival ends the guardian's job outright, the way a ward's coming-of-age ends a guardian's authority.
translation: But now that the faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.

label: Galatians 3:26
text: Paul shifts from "we" (the Jews, under the guardian) to "you" (his readers, Jew and Gentile alike) to signal that the wall dividing them is down. "Children" is huios, "son" in the sense of one who has reached full legal standing, someone who has outgrown the guardian's supervision entirely, not merely a family member by birth.
translation: For you are all sons of God, through faith, in Christ Jesus.

label: Galatians 3:27
text: "Baptized" is baptizo, "to place or put into," describing the Spirit's act of placing a believer into living union with Christ, not the rite of water baptism, which never accomplished this. "Put on" (endyno) is garment language: not a costume or disguise, but stepping into an actual new identity and relationship.
translation: For as many of you as were placed into Christ have put on Christ.

label: Galatians 3:28
text: The three paired opposites, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, name the deepest social divisions of the ancient world and declare them dissolved at the level that matters: shared life "in Christ Jesus," continuing the incorporation language of the previous verse.
translation: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

label: Galatians 3:29
text: Paul closes the chapter's argument with a tight syllogism: belonging to Christ makes you Abraham's seed, since Christ himself is that seed, per verse 16, and therefore an heir, but specifically an heir according to promise, not law.
translation: And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, heirs according to promise.

label: Galatians 4:1–2
text: "Child" translates nepios, a word built from a root meaning "non-speaking" — someone too immature to speak for himself, hence a minor rather than an adult. Paul's legal picture is precise: an heir who is still a nepios has no more practical freedom than a doulos, a slave, even though he technically owns the whole estate. He answers to two different overseers — the epitropos, guardian of his person, and the oikonomos, steward of his property — until prothesmia arrives, a term from Greek inheritance law for the date the father himself fixed in advance for the minority to end. Israel under law, Paul is arguing, occupied exactly this position: heir to everything, yet functionally indistinguishable from a slave until the appointed time.
translation: Now I say that as long as the heir is a child, he differs not at all from a slave, though he is master of everything, but he is under guardians and stewards until the day set beforehand by the father.

label: Galatians 4:3
text: The same word nepios from verse 1 recurs — "children" really means "immature ones." "Elements" is stoicheia, a term for the basic, rudimentary units from which a larger system is assembled — alphabet letters, first principles, starting points. Applied to religion, it points to the elementary stage common to fallen humanity generally, whether that meant the ceremonial machinery of Judaism for the Jew or the ritual observances of paganism for the Gentile.
translation: In the same way we too, when we were immature ones, were held in continual bondage under the elementary principles of the world.

label: Galatians 4:4
text: "The fullness of the time" uses chronos, the Greek word for time simply as duration, a stretch running its course — not kairos, the word for a divinely marked, critical moment. Paul's point is that an appointed span of ordinary time had to run out before God acted. "Sent forth" is the double compound exapostello: apostello alone means to commission an envoy with credentials, the root of our word "apostle"; the prefixed ex adds "out from" — the Son was dispatched out from the Father's own presence, not merely sent on an errand. "Under the law" carries no definite article in the Greek — not merely under the Mosaic code as an institution, but under law as a condition, the ordinary status any Jew was born into.
translation: But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, made under law.

label: Galatians 4:5
text: "Redeem" translates exagorazo, a marketplace verb meaning to buy someone clear out of the slave market. "Adoption" is huiothesia, literally "son-placing" — not, as in modern usage, taking in someone else's child, but the formal installing of a minor into the full legal standing of an adult son, with all rights of inheritance activated at once.
translation: So that he might buy out of slavery those who were under law, so that we might receive the placing as sons.

label: Galatians 4:6
text: "Crying" is krazo, a verb for a loud, unrestrained cry rather than a murmur — in the Greek Old Testament it's often the language of someone crying out to God in urgent prayer. Paul sets the Aramaic Abba directly beside its Greek equivalent, pater — the pairing suggests this may be the very word Jesus himself used in addressing the Father, carried over by his followers with the same warmth and familiarity.
translation: And because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.

label: Galatians 4:7
text: Paul switches from plural "sons" to singular "son," turning the argument from the group to the individual reader — this is now personal, not general. As son, each believer is also kleronomos, heir, and the inheritance rests entirely on that sonship, not on works performed under law.
translation: So that you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then also an heir through God.

label: Galatians 4:8
text: "Did service" translates douloo, the verb form of doulos, "slave" — the identical slavery vocabulary Paul has been using throughout. He isn't denying that the pagan gods existed; he's denying that they are theoi phusei, "gods by nature." Phusis means what belongs to a being by its very origin and essential character. Real, in Paul's view, but not divine — some other class of being altogether.
translation: But at that time, not knowing God, you were enslaved to those which by nature are not gods.

label: Galatians 4:9
text: "Known" is ginosko, a verb for personal, relational knowledge rather than bare intellectual acquaintance — to be "known by God" means to have been the object of his saving initiative, not merely observed by him. "How" opens a genuine cry of astonishment, not a request for information. "Turn" is present tense — this defection was happening even as Paul wrote, not something already completed and past. Two different words lie behind the English "again": one for simple repetition, and a second, sharper one meaning repetition that returns all the way to where you started — Paul's charge is not just that they're repeating an act but sliding clear back to where they began.
translation: But now, having come to know God — or rather, having been known by God — how is it that you are turning back again to the weak and beggarly elementary principles, to which you want to be enslaved all over again?

label: Galatians 4:10
text: "Observe" translates paratereo, a verb for anxious, scrupulous watching — the nervous attentiveness of someone tracking every date lest a prescribed observance slip by unnoticed. The fourfold list — days, months, seasons, years — sweeps in the entire Jewish sacred calendar, from the weekly Sabbath up through the sabbatical and jubilee years.
translation: Days you are scrupulously watching, and months, and seasons, and years.

label: Galatians 4:11
text: "Labour" is kopiao, labor pushed to the point of exhaustion, and it stands in the perfect tense — Paul isn't describing ongoing toil but looking back at a finished, thorough piece of work that may now be wasted. The grammar of his fear suggests he suspects the worst has already happened, not merely that it might.
translation: I am afraid for you, that somehow I have labored over you to the point of exhaustion for nothing.

label: Galatians 4:12
text: "Be" translates ginomai, "become" — not a static state but a change undergone. Paul isn't asking the Galatians to hold still; he's asking them to make the same move he already made, becoming free of the law, because he himself became like a Gentile in order to reach Gentiles.
translation: Become as I am, because I also became as you are, brothers, I beg you. You did me no wrong.

label: Galatians 4:13
text: Paul's phrasing points directly to a physical illness that brought him to preach in Galatia in the first place — the plain sense of the Greek is that sickness, not strategy, put him there.
translation: But you know that it was because of a weakness of the flesh that I preached the gospel to you on that first occasion.

label: Galatians 4:14
text: "Despised" is ekptuo, literally "spit out" — the physical gesture of disgust, not a mild dislike. "Rejected" is exoutheneo, to count as absolutely worthless. Paul's condition, whatever it was, was severe enough to invite exactly that reaction, and the Galatians refused it, receiving him instead as though he were a messenger sent from God, even as Christ Jesus himself.
translation: And the trial that was in my flesh you did not spit out in disgust, nor did you utterly despise it, but you received me as a messenger of God, as Christ Jesus.

label: Galatians 4:15
text: "Blessedness" is makarios, a word that in ordinary Greek usage describes not a pious feeling but a state of flourishing, of prosperity. Paul is asking, quite bluntly, what became of that thriving condition, given how far the Galatians had once been willing to go on his behalf.
translation: Where then is that prosperous blessing of yours? For I bear you witness that, if it had been possible, you would have dug out your own eyes and given them to me.

label: Galatians 4:16
text: "Enemy" translates echthros, a word for active hostility rather than mere estrangement — and Paul insists the label describes only how the Galatians now perceive him, provoked by nothing more than his telling them the truth.
translation: So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

label: Galatians 4:17
text: "Zealously affect" is zeloo, used elsewhere of a suitor pressing attention on someone he's trying to win — the Judaizers are courting the Galatians, working hard at it, but "not well" (kalos), that is, not honorably. The purpose clause exposes the maneuver: they mean to shut the Galatians out — ekkleio, "to shut out" — presumably cutting them off from Paul's gospel of grace, precisely so the Galatians will have nowhere left to turn but back to them.
translation: They are zealously courting you, but not honestly; they want to shut you out, so that you will be courting them.

label: Galatians 4:18–19
text: "My little children" translates teknon, "born ones," a word that stresses the birth relation, and grammatically it sits in apposition rather than as a fresh address — Paul's emotion is overflowing mid-sentence, not starting a new thought. He pictures himself in labor pains again, pointing back to the anguish of first bringing them to faith, until Christ is morphoo — given outward form, outward expression — in them. The passive voice matters: Christ already dwells within them; the problem is that nothing of him shows on the outside, because the Galatians have traded dependence on the Spirit for self-effort under law.
translation: But it is good to be zealously courted in a good thing at all times, and not only when I am present with you, my little children born of me, for whom I am again undergoing birth pains until Christ is outwardly formed in you.

label: Galatians 4:20
text: "Now" is not the ordinary nun but arti, "at this very moment" — a sharper, more immediate marker of time than the plain word would give. "Stand in doubt" is aporeo, built from a word for "a way through" with a negating prefix — literally "without a way," at a loss which direction to take. The verb's middle voice locates the confusion inside Paul himself, a mind pulled back and forth, not merely a difficult set of circumstances outside him.
translation: I could wish to be present with you at this very moment, and to change my tone, because I am without a way forward concerning you.

label: Galatians 4:21
text: "Law" here carries no definite article — Paul isn't narrowly pointing at the Mosaic code but at law as a governing principle of life, the very thing the Galatians are eager to place themselves under. His question functions as a challenge: if you're so devoted to law, have you actually listened to what it says?
translation: Tell me, you who want to be under law, are you not listening to the law?

label: Galatians 4:22
text: "Bondmaid" translates paidiske, the standard Greek term for a female slave. Paul sets the two mothers up as representative figures before drawing out what each line of descent means.
translation: For it stands written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.

label: Galatians 4:23
text: "Was born" stands in the perfect tense rather than the simple past — Paul isn't just reporting a historical fact but pointing to its lasting result, still standing. Ishmael came kata sarka, "according to the flesh," by nature's ordinary working; Isaac came dia epangelias, "through promise," by God's own intervention when nature alone could not have produced him.
translation: But the son of the slave woman has been born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman has been born through the promise.

label: Galatians 4:24
text: "Allegory" doesn't cast doubt on the history — Paul treats the Genesis narrative as literal fact that also carries a further, figurative meaning laid on top of it. He lines up two covenants: the one from Sinai bears children (the same birth-verb used of Ishmael and Isaac) into slavery — and that covenant, he says, is Hagar.
translation: These things contain an allegory. For these women are two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery — this is Hagar.

label: Galatians 4:25
text: The name Hagar apparently echoed the Arabic name for Sinai itself, so the identification isn't arbitrary wordplay but draws on a real geographic association — tying the mountain of the law to the slave-mother, and by extension to the Jerusalem of Paul's own day, still living under the law's bondage.
translation: Now this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she corresponds to the Jerusalem that now is, for she is in slavery with her children.

label: Galatians 4:26
text: "Jerusalem above" was already a familiar category among Jewish teachers, who spoke of a heavenly Jerusalem standing as the archetype behind the earthly city. Paul claims that category for the church — free, and "our mother," set over against the enslaved earthly Jerusalem of the previous verse.
translation: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

label: Galatians 4:27
text: The verse is a direct quotation of Isaiah 54:1, applied here to Sarah, once barren, who stands for the heavenly Jerusalem.
translation: For it stands written: Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break out and cry aloud, you who are not in labor, because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.

label: Galatians 4:28
text: The better manuscripts read "you" rather than "we," addressing the Galatians directly. "After the manner of Isaac" ties their status not to physical descent from Abraham but to the same miraculous promise that produced Isaac.
translation: Now you, brothers, are children of promise, after the manner of Isaac.

label: Galatians 4:29
text: "Persecuted" is imperfect tense, describing ongoing action rather than a single incident — Ishmael's mockery of Isaac was a sustained pattern, matching the sustained pressure the Judaizers were putting on the Galatians.
translation: But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh was continually persecuting the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now also.

label: Galatians 4:30
text: Paul quotes Genesis directly: the rejection of Ishmael becomes, in his reading, the pattern for the rejection of law-keeping as a ground of inheritance.
translation: But what does the Scripture say? Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall by no means inherit with the son of the free woman.

label: Galatians 4:31
text: The verse closes the allegory with a plain declaration, setting up the practical exhortation that follows in chapters five and six.
translation: So then, brothers, we are not children of a slave woman but of the free woman.

label: Galatians 5:1
text: "Freedom" stands in the dative of advantage — Christ's purpose in setting believers free was for their own benefit. "Stand fast" is a present imperative, calling for continuous standing, not a single act, while "be entangled" is a present imperative that's negated — "stop being held" — implying the Galatians were already partway into the net when Paul wrote. "Entangled" translates enecho, "held within," the language of something caught and unable to work itself free.
translation: For this freedom Christ set you free. Keep on standing firm, then, and stop being held again in a yoke of slavery.

label: Galatians 5:2
text: The conditional verb is present tense, "if you keep on being circumcised" — the Galatians had not yet taken the step; Paul is warning them off something still being decided, not rebuking something already done.
translation: Look, I, Paul, say to you that if you keep on being circumcised, Christ will profit you not at all.

label: Galatians 5:3
text: "Testify" is marturomai, a stronger word than ordinary witnessing — closer to a solemn protest. The participle for "circumcised" is present tense, aimed at anyone in the act of receiving the rite, not at those already done — the warning is preventive. "Debtor" is opheiletes, someone bound by obligation: submit to circumcision, and the contract is for the whole law, not just its more comfortable parts.
translation: And I solemnly affirm again to every man who is having himself circumcised, that he is obligated to keep the whole law.

label: Galatians 5:4
text: "Become of no effect" combines katargeo with the preposition "from" — the sense is being cut off from a source, losing the benefit that flows through a connection, not being annihilated. "Fallen from grace" uses ekpipto, "to lose one's grip on, to fail of" — the image is of losing hold of something you had been grasping, not of forfeiting a legal standing already secured once for all.
translation: You have been severed from Christ, you who are seeking to be justified by law; you have lost your hold on grace.

label: Galatians 5:5
text: "Wait" is the same word used elsewhere of the believer's eager expectation of Christ's return — a straining, forward-leaning anticipation, not passive patience. Paul insists this hoped-for righteousness comes "through the Spirit," "by faith" — the opposite path from the self-effort of law-keeping.
translation: For we, through the Spirit, by faith, are eagerly waiting for the hope of righteousness.

label: Galatians 5:6
text: "Availeth" is ischuo, "to have power to accomplish something" — neither the physical mark of circumcision nor its absence carries any power in itself. What has power is faith, and specifically faith actively working itself out through love.
translation: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.

label: Galatians 5:7
text: "Did run" is imperfect tense, picturing a race already underway before something broke its rhythm. "Hinder" translates enkopto, literally "cut in" — the image of another runner breaking into your lane and disrupting your stride, exactly what the Judaizers did to the Galatians' progress.
translation: You were running well. Who cut in on you, to keep you from obeying the truth?

label: Galatians 5:8
text: "Persuasion" is an active-sense noun describing the pressure exerted on the Galatians by the Judaizers' arguments — Paul flatly denies that pressure has any connection to the God who called them.
translation: This persuasion did not come from the one who is calling you.

label: Galatians 5:9
text: The verb "leavens" is present tense — the corruption was underway but had not yet run its full course. Paul's alarm is at the insidious nature of the influence, not merely at how far it had already spread.
translation: A little leaven leavens the whole lump.

label: Galatians 5:10
text: The pronoun "I" is emphatic in the Greek, setting Paul's own confidence apart from whatever anyone else may think. "Confidence" is a perfect-tense form of the verb "to persuade" — a settled conviction already reached and still held, not a fresh guess. "Bear his judgment" uses bastazo, the verb for carrying something genuinely heavy.
translation: I myself have come to a settled confidence in the Lord concerning you, that you will take no other view. But the one who is troubling you will carry his judgment, whoever he is.

label: Galatians 5:11
text: "Yet" implies a contrast with an earlier state of affairs — Paul, as a Pharisee, once did preach circumcision, before his conversion. The condition is contrary to fact: he isn't doing so now, and his ongoing persecution proves it — were he still preaching the law's requirement, the cross would no longer be a skandalon, a "stumbling block," to the Jews who resent it precisely because it sets the law aside.
translation: But I, brothers, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Then the stumbling block of the cross has been done away with.

label: Galatians 5:12
text: "Cut off" is apokopto, a verb for physical mutilation — Paul's biting wish is that those pressing circumcision on the Galatians would go all the way and mutilate themselves entirely, a jab sharpened by the fact that self-castration was practiced by pagan priests in that very region.
translation: I wish that those who are upsetting you would even mutilate themselves.

label: Galatians 5:13
text: "Occasion" is aphorme, a military term for a base of operations, a staging ground for a campaign — Paul warns against turning freedom into exactly that kind of springboard for self-indulgence. "Serve" is, ironically, slave-vocabulary — freedom from the law's slavery is meant to be exchanged for a willing, loving slavery to one another, and the imperative is present tense: keep on serving, continually.
translation: For you were called to freedom, brothers — only do not turn your freedom into a base of operations for the flesh, but through love keep on serving one another.

label: Galatians 5:14
text: "Fulfilled" is a perfect-tense verb, "to fill up, complete" — the tense signals a settled, standing result: the whole law, Paul says, already stands fully met in this one command.
translation: For the whole law stands fulfilled in one statement: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

label: Galatians 5:15
text: The three verbs — bite, devour, consume — are drawn from the vocabulary of wild animals tearing at one another, a startlingly savage picture for describing conflict among Christians.
translation: But if you are biting and devouring one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

label: Galatians 5:16
text: "Walk" is ordinary language for conducting oneself day to day. "Fulfil" is teleo, "carry through to completion," and the Greek stacks two negatives together, which in Greek intensify rather than cancel each other — this is an emphatic promise, not a bare command: walk by the Spirit, and the flesh's desire simply will not be carried through to completion.
translation: But I say, keep on walking by the Spirit, and you will positively not carry out the desire of the flesh.

label: Galatians 5:17
text: "Against" carries the sense of "down upon," pressing to suppress. "Contrary" is a verb meaning "to lie opposed to," and the reciprocal pronoun shows the opposition runs both directions: flesh presses against Spirit, Spirit presses against flesh, each working to keep the other from getting its way in you.
translation: For the flesh continually desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, and these lie opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish.

label: Galatians 5:18
text: "Led" is present tense — ongoing submission to the Spirit's guidance, not a single past transfer of allegiance.
translation: But if you are being led by the Spirit continually, you are not under law.

label: Galatians 5:19
text: "Manifest" is phaneros, "out in the open" — Paul assumes his readers already recognize this list on sight, without needing it explained. "Lasciviousness" is a stronger word than simple sensuality — it describes a shameless, brazen disregard for restraint or public decency, the attitude of someone who no longer cares who's watching.
translation: Now the works of the flesh are plainly evident, and they are things such as these: sexual immorality, impurity, brazen shamelessness.

label: Galatians 5:20
text: "Witchcraft" is pharmakia, the same root behind our word "pharmacy" — sorcery practiced by means of drugs and potions. "Heresies" is hairesis, built from the verb "to choose" — literally a chosen course, a faction gathered around a preferred opinion rather than the truth as given.
translation: Idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambitions, divisions, factions.

label: Galatians 5:21
text: "Do" translates a verb for habitual practice rather than an isolated act — Paul's warning targets settled character, the pattern of a life, not a single lapse. "Revellings" describes the raucous, torch-lit drinking processions that wound through the streets late into the night.
translation: Envyings, drunkenness, carousings, and things like these — about which I warn you in advance, just as I warned you before, that those who habitually practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

label: Galatians 5:22–23
text: "Fruit" is singular, not plural — Paul pictures one unified organic cluster, not nine separate virtues to be cultivated one by one. "Faith" here means faithfulness, reliability — a Spirit-produced trait of character, not the initial act of trusting Christ. "Temperance" is the same word used elsewhere for an athlete's disciplined mastery over his own body in training — self-control in a literal, muscular sense.
translation: But the fruit of the Spirit is: love, joy, peace, patient endurance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-mastery. Against such things there is no law.

label: Galatians 5:24
text: "Crucified" is aorist tense, marking a decisive, completed act rather than an ongoing process — something settled once for all at the moment of faith. Paul pairs two words for the flesh's inner life: one for the passive dispositions and propensities lying within it, and a second for the active reaching-out of those propensities toward gratification.
translation: And those who belong to Christ Jesus crucified the flesh once for all, together with its passions and its cravings.

label: Galatians 5:25
text: "Walk" here is a different verb from the one in verse 16 — one that means "to walk in a straight line, to keep in step," almost a marching term. Since the Spirit is already the source of the believer's life, Paul's logic follows directly: keep that life in step with the source that produces it.
translation: Since we are being kept alive by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

label: Galatians 5:26
text: "Vain glory" is kenodoxos, literally "empty opinion" — a self-estimate with nothing solid behind it, the kind of ungrounded pride that is quick to provoke others and quick to envy them, because it is never secure in itself.
translation: Let us not become those with empty pride, provoking one another, envying one another.

label: Galatians 6:1
text: "Overtaken" is prolambano, "to catch unawares, to take by surprise" — the picture is of a believer surprised into sin, not one who planned it. "Fault" is paraptoma, "a false step, a slip beside the path" — a lighter word than the "transgression" used earlier in the letter for a deliberate stepping over a boundary. "Restore" is katartizo, the word for setting a dislocated bone or mending a torn net — repair that returns something to full working order. "Considering thyself" uses a verb meaning "to fix the eye on, to keep close watch" — the one doing the restoring is told to keep just as sharp an eye on his own footing.
translation: Brothers, even if a man is caught off guard in some false step, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself closely, lest you too be tempted.

label: Galatians 6:2
text: "Bear" is bastazo, the verb for carrying something genuinely heavy — and here the carrying is meant to be willing and sympathetic, not the grudging endurance the same verb can describe elsewhere. "The law of Christ" carries the definite article in Greek, giving it an official ring, as though Christ himself issued this one command — love — as his own governing statute.
translation: Keep on bearing one another's burdens, and so you will fully satisfy the law of the Christ.

label: Galatians 6:3
text: The self-deception in view is simple: a self-estimate detached from reality collapses the moment it's tested, and the one holding it is the last to notice.
translation: For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.

label: Galatians 6:4
text: "Prove" is dokimazo, "to put to the test in order to approve" — an examination aimed at establishing genuine worth, not a snap judgment. "Rejoicing" is kauchema, a legitimate ground for satisfaction measured against oneself alone, not against a neighbor.
translation: But let each one test his own work, and then he will have a reason for exulting with regard to himself alone, and not with regard to the other person.

label: Galatians 6:5
text: The word for "burden" here differs from the one in verse 2, though the distinction shouldn't be pressed too hard in this passage — the paradox is deliberate: bear each other's heavy loads, and yet each remains answerable for his own.
translation: For each will carry his own load.

label: Galatians 6:6
text: "Taught" translates katecheo, literally "to sound down into the ear" — ordinary language for oral instruction, and the root of our word "catechize." "Communicate" is koinoneo, "to hold in partnership with" — the one being taught is to stay in active fellowship with the teacher in every good thing taught, not drift off toward another source of instruction.
translation: Let the one who is being instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.

label: Galatians 6:7
text: "Mocked" is mukterizo, literally "to turn up the nose at" — the picture of a contemptuous sneer, of thinking one can outwit God while wearing a face of outward respect.
translation: Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, this he will also reap.

label: Galatians 6:8
text: "To" in both phrases translates a preposition meaning "with a view to" — not seed literally dropped into soil, but a course of conduct chosen with an eye toward a particular goal, either gratifying the flesh or answering to the Spirit.
translation: Because the one who sows with a view to his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows with a view to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

label: Galatians 6:9
text: "Be weary" pictures a farmer's flagging resolve, worn down by the sheer length of the labor. "Faint" is used elsewhere of reapers physically overcome by heat and exhaustion in the field — both verbs describe the temptation to quit not from one crisis but from the accumulated weight of ongoing effort.
translation: And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give out from exhaustion.

label: Galatians 6:10
text: "Opportunity" is the same word translated "season" in the verse before — a fitting, appointed moment. "Do" is a verb emphasizing sustained, repeated activity rather than a single deed — the call is to keep working good continually, not perform it once and stop.
translation: So then, as we have opportunity, let us keep on working what is good toward all, and especially toward those of the household of the faith.

label: Galatians 6:11
text: Paul draws attention to the size of his own handwriting here — large letters, in contrast to a scribe's smaller hand. Whatever exactly caused it, the detail underlines that these closing words are his own, unmediated, a personal seal on everything the letter has argued.
translation: See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.

label: Galatians 6:12
text: "Make a fair show" translates a compound built plainly from the words for "good" and "face" — to put on a good face, a pleasing outward appearance. The drive to compel circumcision was cosmetic, aimed at the Judaizers' own standing with a watching Jewish audience, not at the truth of the gospel.
translation: As many as want to make a good showing in the flesh, these are trying to compel you to be circumcised, only so that they will not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.

label: Galatians 6:13
text: Paul's charge is pointed: the very people pressing circumcision on the Galatians don't keep the law themselves — their real aim is to boast in the Galatians' flesh, not to honor the law they claim to champion.
translation: For not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves, but they want you to be circumcised so that they may glory in your flesh.

label: Galatians 6:14
text: "Crucified" here stands in the perfect tense — not a past event merely remembered but a standing, settled condition: the old order remains, permanently, a crucified thing to Paul, and he to it.
translation: But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world stands crucified to me, and I to the world.

label: Galatians 6:15
text: Paul states his reason for glorying only in the cross: the mark on the body settles nothing either way; only a genuinely new creation counts.
translation: For neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

label: Galatians 6:16
text: "Rule" is kanon, literally a measuring rod or standard used to check straightness — Paul sets the cross, and a life ordered by the Spirit, as the one standard defining the true Israel of God.
translation: And as many as order their conduct by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.

label: Galatians 6:17–18
text: "Marks" is stigma, the brand burned into the skin of a slave or temple attendant to show which master owned him. Paul's scars from beatings and stoning are, in his own reading, exactly that kind of brand — visible proof of whose he is.
translation: From now on, let no one trouble me, for I bear on my body the brand-marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
